title: Avisa Residences: the promise of a growing township.
videoTitle: PROPERTY REVIEW #367 | AVISA RESIDENCES, TROPICANA ALAM PUNCAK ALAM
excerpt: A double-storey terrace on individual title, planned with the discipline of a strata scheme — arriving at a moment when the highways, the university and the shops are already finished.
takeaways: The site planning does the quiet work: spinal roads so no house faces a junction, cul-de-sacs for privacy, and a single controlled entrance.
Individual title buys total freedom to extend, at the cost of back lanes that stay dead space and a township that drifts out of visual step.
Sean rates the timing above the product — the highways, university, hospital and shops were finished before the houses arrived.

sections.heading: Where Puncak Alam sits now
paragraphs: Sean sets his coordinates before anything else. The site sits near the university campus and its teaching hospital, ringed by a cluster of large established townships that arrived here over the past decade. Tropicana Alam is the newest addition to a location that is no longer remote.

Access is the reason. The Guthrie Corridor Expressway carries most traffic in, running past the university on roads he describes as already sophisticated, with the DASH highway and other new links connecting onward toward the city and the coast. He is blunt that this location was once the butt of his own jokes about being too far out, and that the highways changed the argument entirely.
The wider master plan runs to about 362 acres on leasehold land. Avisa Residences is the first phase — roughly 911 units across 88 acres of it.

sections.heading: A site plan doing quiet work
paragraphs: What impresses Sean is the planning discipline, which he attributes to a developer that has built this product repeatedly across earlier townships. A public lake at the entrance doubles as the water retention structure and as a place-making gesture, open to everyone rather than fenced into the scheme.

Inside, there is a single way in and out past a guard house, with a roundabout separating the two phases. The roads are laid out so that no unit faces a junction head-on, and phase two adds cul-de-sacs so only residents of that street ever drive down it.

Perimeter fencing and planting wrap the boundary, and shared facilities — courts and park space — sit in the centre, so the first thing a resident sees on the way home is open landscape rather than rows of parked cars.

sections.heading: Reading a landed unit from the kerb
paragraphs: Before entering, Sean applies his standard landed checklist from the pavement. He looks at where the drains sit and which way surface water will run in heavy rain, at the broom-finished walkway texture, and at the small landscape island out front — noting that on individual title, most owners will eventually pave over it anyway.

The intermediate unit is a 20 by 70 lot of about 1,917 sq ft with four bedrooms and three bathrooms. A second type shares the dimensions but carries a larger built-up of roughly 1,991 sq ft, with the ground-floor kitchen fully extended to the boundary. That single difference is the entire choice on offer, which he defends: on individual title, buyers will extend to their own taste anyway, so more variants would be wasted.

The car porch is finished in imprinted concrete with expansion joints, at about 2.8 m, and carries no column in the middle — so two cars park without the awkward pillar most owners end up demolishing. Letterbox, external water filter position and a generously sized refuse compartment are gathered to one side.

sections.heading: The constraint every terrace house fights
paragraphs: Sean pauses to explain the structural problem of an intermediate terrace: you only get two facades, front and back. Everything else is shared party wall, so architects push as much glazing as possible into those two faces — here a 20 ft frontage with a sliding door around 2.7 m wide — and then look for a third source of light through the roof.

Inside, the door clearance is about 900 mm and the entrance foyer 2.18 m across, with the door set slightly off to leave room for a sideboard. His first criticism lands immediately: the soffit at the entry drops to roughly 2.45 m because the bathroom above needs depth for its pipework.

Past it the space recovers. The living and dining run open with no columns or beams interrupting them, under a 2.98 m ceiling, roughly 4.8 m from staircase to wall, on 600 mm tiles with matching skirting. He returns to the low box-up near the stair and argues it is not fully structural and could have been tidied — an intimidating line across an otherwise generous room.

sections.heading: Kitchen, yard and the room downstairs
paragraphs: The kitchen runs about 2.43 m wall to wall with 5 ft wall tiling and sockets already positioned for a lower and upper run of cabinets, leading through to a yard with water and power points ready for a washing machine. A wall here means the kitchen can be closed off if the owner wants.

Sean flags a detail most reviews would skip: the flooring changes between the living area and the kitchen. Glossy tiles in the living and dining make the space read larger; a matte tile with more friction goes where water gets spilled. He calls it thoughtful.

The ground-floor bedroom measures about 3.25 m by 3.2 m — larger, he notes, than the kitchen — and he agrees with that priority, because this is the room that matters when parents move in. Its bathroom is entered over a ramp rather than a step, which he praises for mobility, though he would have preferred a sliding door for exactly the same reason.

sections.heading: The double-height family hall, and its bills
paragraphs: Upstairs is the moment the house is designed around: a family hall rising about 6.1 m to a high window. Sean identifies three jobs it does at once — the immediate impression on arrival, a volume for hot air to rise away from the living spaces, and most importantly daylight from above, solving the terrace house's missing third facade.

He is equally clear about what it costs. Nobody will clean those windows until they sell the house years later. Installing a ceiling fan or light up there requires scaffolding, which means extra cost during the move-in, and a different specification of fan.

His design suggestion is specific: a louvred window rather than a top-hinged one, so air and daylight still come through while birds and driven rain stay out. He also prefers an extended handrail to the solid parapet wall at the landing, which would open the space and probably install faster.

sections.heading: Bedrooms, and why the corner lot costs more
paragraphs: The two rear bedrooms measure roughly 2.79 by 3.8 m and 3.2 by 2.9 m, sharing a bathroom, both taking a queen bed with room left for a wardrobe and desk. The master runs about 4 m wall to wall with a large front window, an area that converts easily into a walk-in wardrobe, and an ensuite with the same toe-friendly ramp.

Then Sean walks the corner unit, and the difference is not subtle. At 22 by 70 it is only slightly wider, but the extra side facade changes everything: a private side garden, more flexible bedroom windows upstairs, and an ensuite for every bedroom. Because the side windows bring their own daylight, the family hall no longer needs the tall void.

Pricing discussed in the episode put intermediate units in the six-hundred-thousands and the corner unit above nine hundred thousand, reflecting the recording date and the specific types shown. His verdict on landed economics is unchanged: corner, end and intermediate, with scarcity doing the work at the corner.

sections.heading: Factories, freedom and the homework
paragraphs: His concerns begin with tenure. This is leasehold on a landed product, which matters to a large group of conventional Malaysian buyers, and he says so plainly.

His second reservation is individual title itself, which he admits is personal. The back lane between rows stays dead space — dark at night, facing everyone's exhaust and washing — where a strata scheme would have landscaped it into a park. And the freedom to extend means that in five years the township will have drifted out of visual step with itself. Good if you want to do whatever you like with your house; less good if you value a coherent street.

The third is the surroundings, and he presents both sides. Industrial lots sit opposite, bringing heavy vehicles and occasional production noise — but also jobs, and fewer competing homes than if those plots held apartments. He advises choosing orientation deliberately, since some rows sit nearer the factories and others nearer the hills. Above all he notes how much competition this budget now faces here, and tells buyers to do the comparison work.
Individual-title terrace houses inside a guarded, single-entry master plan.
Highways, UiTM and shops are already in place in Puncak Alam.
Leasehold title and factories across the road are the main trade-offs.

sections.heading: What sets it apart
paragraphs: Avisa Residences is phase one of Tropicana Alam: 911 double-storey terrace houses on 88 acres with individual titles, yet a single guarded way in and out. Spine roads mean no house faces a junction, and there is a five-acre lake and parks.

The 20 by 70 ft Type A has 1,917 sq ft and four bedrooms, including a ground-floor bedroom with a ramped bathroom for older parents, and a family hall about 6.1 metres high that brings light into the middle of the house. Intermediate units were from about RM600,000; corner units, where every bedroom has its own bathroom, about RM900,000.

sections.heading: Where it is
paragraphs: It is in Puncak Alam beside the UiTM campus and hospital, among established townships such as City of Elmina, Bandar Seri Coalfields and Gamuda Gardens, with the GCE, DASH and WCE highways nearby. Factories are going up across the road.

pros: It is the product most Malaysian buyers want — a double-storey terrace on individual title — but planned inside a master-planned township with a public lake, park and jogging track, and the guarded characteristics of a single controlled entrance.

The timing is unusually good: the expressways, the university and its hospital, the shops and the hypermarket were all finished before the houses, so buyers moving in two or three years from filming inherit none of the incompleteness earlier neighbours complained about.

It sits in a genuine gap in the market — the freedom of individual title, but with a guard house, park and facilities that a free-for-all landed scheme never provides, at pricing he considers competitive against newer projects.
cons: The land is leasehold, which for a landed product still matters to a large group of conventional buyers.

Individual title leaves the back lanes as dead, dark negative space where a strata scheme would have landscaped them, and unrestricted extensions mean the township will lose its visual coherence over time.
Industrial lots directly opposite bring heavy vehicles and production noise, and the sheer number of competing developments in this budget means far more homework before committing.

sections.closing: Avisa's strongest argument is not the house but the sequence: infrastructure, university, hospital and shops all arrived before the keys did. What a buyer trades for that is tenure and the tidiness of a managed street — and whether the freedom to build whatever you want is a feature or a cost is genuinely a matter of temperament.
sections.sourceNote: Based on Sean's full public English captions and his published YouTube episode notes. Measurements, unit sizes and prices are as discussed in the video and reflect the recording date; the units shown were show and advance units. The 3 on 3 section paraphrases the three things Sean says he likes and the three he has concerns about, presented near the end of the episode.

The terrace house Malaysians love, with an individual title, set in a master plan with a lake, parks, a single guarded entry, spine roads and perimeter fencing, from a developer whose earlier Tropicana Aman phases show the same consistency. Owners can extend as they like, which makes corner lots especially desirable.
The timing: the highways, UiTM, the hospital and shops are already there, so by handover in two or three years the area won't feel unfinished, a complaint buyers of earlier nearby projects had.
Competitive pricing: at the edge of the developable land, it undercuts other new projects while offering both the freedom of an individual title and a guardhouse, parks and privacy.

cons: Leasehold title, which matters to many landed buyers, and an individual-title format whose back lanes stay bare and whose look will fragment as owners renovate.
Industrial lots across the road mean heavy vehicles and possible noise, though also jobs and less competing housing; choose your orientation carefully.
So many projects nearby that, at RM600,000 to RM700,000, buyers have a lot of homework comparing them.
closing: Good value for a guarded, individual-title terrace house in a maturing area, if leasehold and the neighbouring factories don't put you off.
sourceNote: Based on Sean's full English captions for this February 2025 episode. The 3 on 3 follows the three things he likes and the three he doesn't, in his order, at the end of the video. The developer's team showed Sean around.
